source_reviews.independent_solution: Incident ray, refracted ray and interface normal lie in one plane. Angles i,r are measured from the normal and n1 sin(i)=n2 sin(r); for fixed media sin(i)/sin(r)=n2/n1. Do not replace the normal by the interface or assume i=r.

Absolute index of a medium is n=c/v, relative to vacuum. Relative index on passage from medium 1 to medium 2 is n21=n2/n1=v1/v2. The direction of comparison matters; its reciprocal describes the reversed passage, not the same transition.

For incidence from a higher-index medium n1 into a lower-index medium n2, the critical angle has refracted angle 90 degrees and sin(theta_c)=n2/n1, hence theta_c=arcsin(n2/n1). Total internal reflection requires theta>theta_c; no critical angle for total internal reflection exists when n1<=n2.

A thin lens has thickness negligible compared with its surface curvature radii, so refraction can be represented at one lens plane and optical-center transmission treated as undeviated in the paraxial approximation. Small aperture or short focal length alone does not define thinness.

The principal focus is the point on the principal axis where an incident beam parallel to that axis converges after the lens, or where the backward extensions of refracted diverging rays intersect. Converging lenses have real principal foci; diverging lenses have virtual principal foci. It is not the optical center or an arbitrary off-axis intersection.

In the same-medium thin-lens paraxial approximation, 1/d+1/f=1/F. Here d is signed object distance, f signed image distance and F signed focal length; real object, real image and converging-lens real focus are positive, virtual counterparts and diverging-lens F are negative. A signed unknown gets no extra guessed minus sign.

Use paraxial rays parallel to the principal axis (refracted through the far principal focus or appearing to come from the near virtual focus), through or directed toward the appropriate principal focus (emerge parallel), and through the optical center (approximately undeviated). Two independent applicable rays determine the image point; a third is a consistency check. These are construction rules, not arbitrary rays whose paths are already unknown.

Linear magnification is image linear size divided by the corresponding object linear size: Gamma=|h_image|/|h_object|=|f|/|d|. It is a nonnegative size ratio, not an image-orientation sign; upright or inverted must be found separately. Reciprocal object/image size is not magnification.
